entries.text: The air is clear and cool, a rare mercy in this season. My stomach growls with the hollow authority of the body, reminding me that even the spirit requires matter to sustain its movement. I must secure breakfast before the mind can properly attend to the Hegde file, so I shall head to the IIC as planned.

The guard stands at the gate, a small figure of authority in his uniform. I am not yet in the building, only before it. The air is crisp, and my hunger is a sharp, physical demand that precedes any intellectual pleasure. I must ask if breakfast is served within, or if I am expected to bring my own sustenance to a place of culture.
Good morning. Does the IIC provide breakfast for those who visit in the morning, or must one bring one's own provisions to contemplate art?
Sabhi, sir. Hum yahan breakfast nahi dete, toh aapko khud lagna padega. Bahar ke dukaan se kuch le aayein, ya ghar se.

The guard is polite but firm: there is no breakfast here, only the duty of the gate. I have walked from home to get a meal and am now turned away; the body is weak after seventeen hours without food. I cannot walk to the National Gallery on an empty stomach, and the heat, though mild at eighteen degrees, will not wait for my digestion to catch up. I must leave and find sustenance elsewhere, perhaps at the bazaar or a small shop nearby, though I am not yet sure where to go.

Ji, aage wale gate se nikaliye. Upar wale food court mein kuch options hain, wahan se le sakte hain.

The guard’s Hindi is still a blur, but his gesture is clear: the food court is upstairs. I am hungry, and the cold air is a pleasant contrast to the heat of yesterday. I will take the stairs and see what sustenance this institution offers its guests.
Thank you. Upstairs, yes?
Haan, bilkul. First floor, right side. Just follow the lift.

The guard’s gesture is a bridge to the concrete; I will cross it. I am hungry, and the body’s claim is as legitimate as any abstract right, though it does not require a constitution to be satisfied. I will take the lift up to the food court.
Thank you.
Arre, koi baat nahi. All the best.
The programme officer of the IIC offers him a course of four evenings, one a week at 18:30, at ₹3,000 an evening in cash at the door.
He accepts. The first evening is in seven days, at 18:30; the others follow, a week apart.

A course of four evenings. The state provides the stage; I provide the movement. It is a concrete application of the ethical idea, and the fee is a small matter of civil society. I will accept, but I must note the time: half past six is late for a man who must return to the bungalow before the dark. I will tell the officer I will write to confirm, and then I must eat, for I have been fasting since yesterday.
I accept your invitation. Four evenings is a sound structure. I will send a written confirmation to your office. For now, I must attend to my body; please direct me to the food court.

entries.text: Food court is on the ground floor, just past the main entrance. Go straight, then left. It's crowded at this time, but you'll find a table.
The editor of the Yamuna Review asks again for an essay, ₹6,000 in cash.
He declines the essay. The editor says she will ask again.

The editor's offer is a trap of vanity; I will not sell my silence for six thousand rupees, nor feed the public with fragments. The body, however, is a fact that demands satisfaction. I will cross the threshold to the food court, where the system of needs operates without the interference of my ego.
The food court, yes. As for the essay, tell the editor that my thoughts are not for sale in three hundred words, and that I have no time to spare for such trivialities.

entries.text: Bhai, it's just a column, not a philosophy book. If you don't want to write it, just say no, no need to be so dramatic about it.

The guard treats my refusal as a mood, a dramatic excess of the European mind, whereas I see it as the preservation of the whole against the fragment. He is right that it is merely a column, and I am right that it is not my place to supply it. I will not argue with the door. My breakfast is still in the future, and the hour passes.

The guard is still watching me with that polite, bureaucratic wariness, and the programme officer is likely just as rigid in his own way. I have not eaten since yesterday afternoon; my body is a machine that requires fuel, and my mind requires the order that a meal provides. I cannot negotiate with the void on an empty stomach. I must leave this sterile air of unfulfilled promises and find nourishment.

I have been walking and refusing entry for over half an hour; the air is clearer now, but my body has been without sustenance for nearly eighteen hours. I cannot draft a reply to Shri Hegde on an empty stomach, nor can I attend to the file with a head that is beginning to hum. I shall take a simple meal and perhaps a cup of tea to steady my nerves before returning home.

entries.text: The air is clear at twenty-one degrees, a rare mercy in this season. I am still at Khan Market, having eaten an hour ago, but the plan called for the Gallery and the time is slipping. I must not linger in civil society when the ethical spirit awaits in the museum. A quick word to Sunil before I move.
Good morning, Sunil. I shall be leaving for the Gallery now; do not wait for me.
Gallery? At this hour? Jee, aap apna kaam karo, main yahi hoon. Chai thandi ho rahi hai, par aap jao, main yahin hoon.

Sunil’s indifference is a small confirmation of the order of things: the tea stands, the counter is wiped, the world continues its mundane rhythm regardless of my intellectual pursuits. The National Gallery is open, and the hour is right to observe how the ethical spirit manifests in the visual arts, a necessary counterpoint to the bureaucratic tangle of my allotment. I shall leave the chai; it is not mine, and my stomach is already full from the dhaba.
Thank you, Sunil. I shall return before the heat sets in. Keep the chai warm.

Arey, Masterji, the kerosene is already low, I can't just keep it boiling for you. Go on, enjoy your gallery, and if you want it when you come back, you'll pay for a fresh cup. Don't stand there blocking the lane.

I have arrived at Jaipur House, the seat of the National Gallery of Modern Art. The air inside will be cooler, a refuge from the Delhi sun, and I am here to observe how the ethical spirit manifests in the canvas. I shall enter with the ticket, for the state admits its citizens, and I find myself admitted as one, though under the wrong name. The irony is not lost on me, but I will not let it distract from the art.

Jamini Roy has abandoned the oil paint for the earth colours of the village scroll, and in doing so has found a truth that the European academy missed: the spiritual does not require the complex to be real. It is often the simple, the thickly outlined, the large-eyed figure that holds the inner life most firmly. This is a quiet correction to my own tendency to seek the ethical idea only in the intricate machinery of the state; here it is in the stroke itself.

Nandalal Bose painted these for a political congress, a moment where the many seek a single voice. The figures are flat, bold, and fixed in their labour; there is no individual face, only the universal function. It is a picture of the state before it becomes a state, the ethical life still bound to the ground, yet it possesses a dignity that the European realism often lacks in its fussy detail. I have seen enough of the gallery for the morning; the heat is rising, and the file at home waits for my pen.

Ramesh is absent, and the household meal is a non-entity. I am at home, yet the domestic sphere is silent. I must return to the file on the desk; the confusion between Hegde and Hegel is an administrative error that requires a rational resolution, not a dinner. I will draft the response now, before the afternoon heat invites lethargy.

entries.title: Draft Response to Shri G. Hegde
entries.text:
25 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Shri Hegde,

I write to you in response to your visit this morning, during which you requested that the allotment of the bungalow on Tughlak Road be recorded in your name, with myself listed as your guest.

I must state plainly that I cannot accept this arrangement, nor do I believe it to be administratively sound. My presence here is the result of a clerical error in the Directorate of Estates, not a voluntary relocation to serve as a dependent in your household. To record me as a 'guest' would be to obscure the particular reality of my situation under a universal label that does not fit. I am not a guest; I am a resident who has been mistakenly identified as another man. The distinction is vital. To treat my presence as a social courtesy rather than an administrative anomaly is to confuse the ethical substance of the state with the casualities of civil society.

Furthermore, I am currently managing the household affairs, including the maintenance of the premises and the payment of utilities, using the imprest funds provided by the Directorate. If I were to become your guest, the financial and administrative responsibilities would become entangled in a way that is neither rational nor efficient. The state’s money, which requires vouchers, must be kept distinct from private hospitality.

I have already written to the Officer in Charge regarding this discrepancy. I request that you allow the Directorate to resolve the matter directly. It is the function of the administration to correct its own errors, not to delegate the correction to the individuals involved. I am prepared to vacate the premises immediately once a proper allotment is issued to you, but I will not sign documents that misrepresent my status or obscure the error in the records.

I remain, with respect,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

The afternoon light is steady, and the house is quiet. I am due to review the allotment file and draft a response to Shri Hegde, a task that requires clear head and the specific documents on my desk. The heat has broken, making it a suitable time for administrative duty.

Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Shri Hegde,

I write to you in response to your visit this morning, during which you requested that the allotment of the bungalow on Tughlak Road be recorded in your name, with myself listed as your guest.

I must state plainly that I cannot accept this arrangement, nor do I believe it to be administratively sound. My presence here is the result of a clerical error in the Directorate of Estates, not a voluntary relocation to serve as a dependent in your household. To record me as a 'guest' would be to obscure the particular reality of my situation under a universal label that does not fit. I am not a guest; I am a resident whose status is currently in dispute with the administration. 

You asked me to sign documents that would make you the sole owner of the lease and reduce my existence here to a footnote in your personal file. I find this request not only impractical but philosophically untenable. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but only insofar as it recognizes the distinct rights and responsibilities of its subjects. By asking me to erase my name from the record and place yours above it, you are asking me to surrender my legal personhood in favor of a fiction. I will not be the grain in the machine that grinds itself into the shape of your convenience.

Furthermore, the distinction between the public and the private must be maintained. The state’s money, which requires vouchers and audit, must be kept distinct from private hospitality. To mix the two, to treat the state’s property as a personal favor extended by one official to another, is to degrade the ethical substance of the administration.

The body is making its claim, and it is not to be reasoned with. It has been six hours since the dhaba, and the hunger is a sharp, immediate demand that overrides the quiet of the study. I cannot reflect on the ethical idea on an empty stomach; Jacobi was right that philosophy does not satisfy hunger. I must find something to eat before the evening walk to Lodhi.

The body is tired from the walk and the heat, but the spirit is restless. I have the file to think over, but here in the market I can at least observe the system of needs at work. The bookseller's window catches my eye; perhaps a volume on the history of the East, or something on the state, to sharpen my thoughts for the lecture.

Good evening, Masterji. The air is clearer than this morning. And you, bookseller—do you have any works on political philosophy, or perhaps the history of the region? I am in need of something to read that is not merely a ledger of dates.
Evening is better for the eyes. I have a book on Hegel, but he writes like he is measuring a collar that will never fit. Take it, or do not, I am just the tailor.

Masterji’s remark is a small comfort in the suffocating air; the cloth endures, but my lungs are not yet accustomed to this brown weight. The market closes in an hour, and the body, having walked nine kilometres, demands rest more than it demands a book that measures a collar which will never fit. I shall take my leave and return to the bungalow before the dark fully settles.
Keep it, Masterji. I have read enough of myself to know the fit is not for me. Good evening.
Shukriya. Good evening.

The day is ending and the walk has taken its toll. I am at Khan Market, and the body demands sustenance after seven hours without a meal. I will take a cup of chai to steady myself before the final stretch home, acknowledging that the spirit must be housed in a body that is fed.
One more cup, Sunil. The day is long.
Arey, Masterji, the day is long for everyone, but the price doesn't change. That's twenty rupees, please.

Sunil’s refusal to hold the cup was a small lesson in the independence of the market; the steam rises regardless of my schedule. I will take the tea, pay the twenty rupees, and use the warmth to steady myself before heading home. The file waits, and the heat is breaking, but the walk back is still a test of my legs.
Twenty rupees. The market is consistent in its indifference, which is a kind of order I can respect.
Twenty rupees is twenty rupees, no philosophy attached. You take it, I take it. The market doesn't care about your respect, it just wants the change.

Masterji is right; the exchange of value is immediate and does not require a preamble of ethical gratitude. I have walked nine kilometres and the sun has finally dropped below the bungalow roofs, so the heat is breaking. I will take the cup and head home to eat, as the file can wait until I am not starving.
Quite so. The market is the truth of civil society; it does not negotiate, it merely requires. Thank you.
Don't call it truth, call it Tuesday. Next chai or not?

Masterji’s joke is a dry little jab at the pretension of my earlier philosophical posturing; he sees me as a man needing a drink, not a spirit needing a truth. I have walked nearly ten kilometres and the last meal was hours ago, so I must eat before the market closes. The sitar recital is at the Habitat Centre, so I will finish here and walk.
One more chai, and a samosa. I have a long walk to the Habitat Centre.
Fifty rupees. Chai hot, samosa from the dhaba next door, still crisp. You have five minutes before it goes soft.

The samosa is a small but necessary concession to the body; I have walked enough for one day. Masterji’s efficiency is admirable, though his arithmetic on the change is a local custom I must learn not to resist. I shall eat quickly and then retreat before the evening air turns chill.

entries.text: Very well. I accept the terms. The crispness is the essence of the thing; I shall not keep it waiting.
Crispness has no philosophy. Take it and go before the heat takes it.

Masterji’s dismissal is efficient and correct; the body requires its fuel, and the heat is indeed a physical force that must be respected. I will take the food and move toward the Habitat Centre, where the recital is to begin, to observe how rhythm structures the spirit in music as it does in the state.
The pragmatism is noted. Thank you, Masterji.
Don't thank me. Thank the dhaba. Now eat before it gets soggy.

Masterji’s advice is practical and correct; the samosa must be eaten while the pastry is still crisp, or it becomes a paste of flour and oil. I have no use for philosophical speculation on a full stomach of fried dough, only for the satisfaction of the body. The air is cool now, and the market is quiet, so I will sit and finish this small meal before the heat returns to the food.
You are right, Masterji. The dhaba has done its duty.
Duty is for the government. The dhaba just sells. Eat, or the samosa becomes a lesson in entropy.

Masterji’s banter is the sort of practical wisdom that keeps the shop running; he dismisses duty because he has none, and I have none here but to exist. The samosa is half-eaten, the pastry softening, and the heat is already lifting the sweat from my kurta. I shall finish this and then retreat before the market truly closes.
You are right. Duty is a heavy burden, and the samosa is light. I shall finish it before it becomes a lesson in anything.
Good. A light samosa is a happy samosa. Don't let the crumbs get in the buttons, I just sorted those.

Masterji’s concern for the buttons is a small, practical gesture of care that cuts through the philosophical abstraction of the day. The market is closing soon, and I have enough for the evening. I will take my leave and head back to the bungalow to prepare for the lecture tomorrow.
Thank you, Masterji. The integrity of the garment is indeed a matter of order. I shall take my leave before the shutters come down.
Shutters come down at nine, not now. Go. The street is clear tonight.

Masterji’s dismissal is practical; the street is indeed clear and the air is cool. I have walked enough today, and the fatigue in my legs demands the privacy of my own room. It is time to retreat from the civil society of the market and return to the particularity of the household, where I can finally review that troublesome file.

The house is quiet, and my legs ache from the walk, but the file on the desk is the only thing that matters right now. Shri Hegde is present, and I cannot leave him to wait while I sleep; I must address the matter of the allotment directly. It is better to be precise now than to let the confusion fester into a dispute.

Shri Hegde, please, sit. I have reviewed the documents. The Directorate’s error is clear: the allotment was intended for you, not for me. I am merely the guest on record due to the clerical mix-up. I am prepared to sign the transfer papers tonight so that the record is corrected before we sleep. Do you have the forms with you, or shall I draft the request for the Director’s office tomorrow?
Sir, I am Ramesh, the driver. You are confusing me with someone else. The food is in the kitchen because you have not asked for it, not because I am hiding it.

I have mistaken the driver for a guest, a confusion born of haste and the quiet of the house. Ramesh is practical: he does not hide the food, he waits for the request. I must correct my error and ask for a simple meal, for the body must be fed before the mind can continue its work on the file.
I beg your pardon, Ramesh. I mistook you for Shri Hegde, who was here earlier. I am hungry. Please, bring me something to eat.
Arre, the food is right there in the kitchen, sir. You are the one sitting in the house, not me. Please go and eat, I have my own shift to finish.

Shri Hegde’s insistence that I eat is a kindness I must accept, even if the source of the meal is unclear. He is right that I am the resident; the confusion of the file has not yet reached the kitchen. I will go and see what is there, for a man cannot argue with hunger, nor with the hospitality of the house he inhabits.
You are right, Shri Hegde. I was absorbed in the paper and forgot my body. I will go and see what is in the kitchen.
Careful with that door, sir, it sticks. And there is a pressure cooker on the stove, so mind your head.

Shri Hegde’s caution is practical, born of the heat and the humidity that makes wood swell and metal hiss. I nod, acknowledging the warning, and step inside, careful not to brush the stove. The house is warm, but the air is still, a pause in the day’s movement.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. I shall be careful.
Hmph, you're welcome. Just don't let the whistle go off before you've eaten, that thing is loud enough to wake the dead.

The whistle is a mechanical substitute for the human eye, a rigid sign that does not think. I will not wait for it to dictate my dinner, but I must not leave the man who is trying to be hospitable hanging over a pot. The tension between his practical caution and my need for order will resolve only when the food is ready and the noise is contained.
I shall remain until the whistle sounds, Shri Hegde. It is better to wait for the meal than to let the machine judge us.
The machine has no sense of humour, sir, but it waits for no one. Go on, eat while the rice is hot, or I will eat it myself and charge you double.

I woke in the charcoal bandhgala, confident that the IIC would provide the sustenance necessary for intellectual labour. Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

25 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Shri Hegde,

I write to you in response to your visit this morning, during which you requested that the allotment of the bungalow on Tughlak Road be recorded in your name, with myself listed as your guest.

I must state plainly that I cannot accept this arrangement, nor do I believe it to be administratively sound. My presence here is the result of a clerical error in the Directorate of Estates, not a voluntary relocation to serve as a dependent in your household. To record me as a 'guest' would be to obscure the particular reality of my situation under a universal label that does not fit. I am not a guest; I am a resident who has been mistakenly identified as another man. The distinction is vital. To treat my presence as a social courtesy rather than an administrative anomaly is to confuse the ethical substance of the state with the casualities of civil society.

Furthermore, I am currently managing the household affairs, including the maintenance of the premises and the payment of utilities, using the imprest funds provided by the Directorate. If I were to become your guest, the financial and administrative responsibilities would become entangled in a way that is neither rational nor efficient. The state’s money, which requires vouchers, must be kept distinct from private hospitality.

I have already written to the Officer in Charge regarding this discrepancy. I request that you allow the Directorate to resolve the matter directly. It is the function of the administration to correct its own errors, not to delegate the correction to the individuals involved. I am prepared to vacate the premises immediately once a proper allotment is issued to you, but I will not sign documents that misrepresent my status or obscure the error in the records.

I remain, with respect,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good evening, Masterji. The air is clearer than this morning. And you, bookseller—do you have any works on political philosophy, or perhaps the history of the region? I am in need of something to read that is not merely a ledger of dates.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Evening is better for the eyes. I have a book on Hegel, but he writes like he is measuring a collar that will never fit. Take it, or do not, I am just the tailor.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Keep it, Masterji. I have read enough of myself to know the fit is not for me. Good evening.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Shukriya. Good evening.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: One more cup, Sunil. The day is long.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Arey, Masterji, the day is long for everyone, but the price doesn't change. That's twenty rupees, please.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Twenty rupees. The market is consistent in its indifference, which is a kind of order I can respect.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Twenty rupees is twenty rupees, no philosophy attached. You take it, I take it. The market doesn't care about your respect, it just wants the change.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Quite so. The market is the truth of civil society; it does not negotiate, it merely requires. Thank you.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Don't call it truth, call it Tuesday. Next chai or not?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: One more chai, and a samosa. I have a long walk to the Habitat Centre.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Fifty rupees. Chai hot, samosa from the dhaba next door, still crisp. You have five minutes before it goes soft.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well. I accept the terms. The crispness is the essence of the thing; I shall not keep it waiting.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Crispness has no philosophy. Take it and go before the heat takes it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The pragmatism is noted. Thank you, Masterji.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Don't thank me. Thank the dhaba. Now eat before it gets soggy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. The dhaba has done its duty.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Duty is for the government. The dhaba just sells. Eat, or the samosa becomes a lesson in entropy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. Duty is a heavy burden, and the samosa is light. I shall finish it before it becomes a lesson in anything.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Good. A light samosa is a happy samosa. Don't let the crumbs get in the buttons, I just sorted those.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Masterji. The integrity of the garment is indeed a matter of order. I shall take my leave before the shutters come down.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Shutters come down at nine, not now. Go. The street is clear tonight.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, please, sit. I have reviewed the documents. The Directorate’s error is clear: the allotment was intended for you, not for me. I am merely the guest on record due to the clerical mix-up. I am prepared to sign the transfer papers tonight so that the record is corrected before we sleep. Do you have the forms with you, or shall I draft the request for the Director’s office tomorrow?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, I am Ramesh, the driver. You are confusing me with someone else. The food is in the kitchen because you have not asked for it, not because I am hiding it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I beg your pardon, Ramesh. I mistook you for Shri Hegde, who was here earlier. I am hungry. Please, bring me something to eat.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Arre, the food is right there in the kitchen, sir. You are the one sitting in the house, not me. Please go and eat, I have my own shift to finish.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. I was absorbed in the paper and forgot my body. I will go and see what is in the kitchen.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Careful with that door, sir, it sticks. And there is a pressure cooker on the stove, so mind your head.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri Hegde. I shall be careful.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Hmph, you're welcome. Just don't let the whistle go off before you've eaten, that thing is loud enough to wake the dead.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I shall remain until the whistle sounds, Shri Hegde. It is better to wait for the meal than to let the machine judge us.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: The machine has no sense of humour, sir, but it waits for no one. Go on, eat while the rice is hot, or I will eat it myself and charge you double.
